paras: The Onancock wharf riot was a fight on August 17, 1890, at the steamboat wharf in Onancock, Accomack County, Virginia, between white townsmen and Black excursionists from Baltimore boarding the steamer Helen after a camp meeting. Stones, bricks and pistols were used, and two papers reported at least three Black passengers shot or struck, while a Baltimore German paper said no one was known to be wounded. No arrests were reported, and the Richmond Dispatch presented the affair as "A NEGRO OUTRAGE."

The Helen, under Captain Smith of the Eastern Shore Line, left Baltimore on Saturday night, August 16, with about four hundred Black excursionists bound for a camp meeting. The Dispatch's Onancock correspondent placed the "colored Methodist camp-meeting" at Savageville, two miles south of the town, and said a committee headed by Philip Finney, formerly of Accomac, had chartered the steamer. Both the Evening Star and the Dispatch said the passengers drank heavily on the way down, and the Dispatch added that some fought with clubs, knives and razors at the camp ground.

On Sunday afternoon the excursionists gathered at the Onancock wharf to board the steamer for the return trip. Accounts of how the trouble began differ, but in each a white man's blow or the white men's thrown bricks opened the general fight. According to the Evening Star, the passengers smashed the steamer's chairs and hurled the pieces at the whites on the wharf, who sent stones through the cabin windows.

The Evening Star reported that one Black man was shot through the right shoulder, two others had their heads split open by stones, and several white men were slightly hurt. The Alexandria Gazette put the white crowd at "about fifty" and said a Black man and a Black woman were struck by missiles and another Black man was shot through the hand. In the Dispatch's version, Black passengers fired pistols at the whites, who answered with brickbats that knocked some of the passengers down, while the town sergeant tried in vain to stop the fight. Captain Smith cut loose early, leaving behind more than one hundred excursionists by the Dispatch's count.

The Dispatch reported "the most intense excitement" in the town afterward and said it was fortunate for the passengers that the steamer had already gone. Mayor Taylor of Onancock telegraphed the Baltimore chief of police to arrest the ringleaders when the steamer arrived. The Evening Star said the passengers hurried away on landing and no arrests were made. No report of later charges or an inquiry appears in the coverage.

All of the coverage came from white newspapers on August 19 and 22; no Black newspaper report appears. The Dispatch printed the longest account, headed "A NEGRO OUTRAGE" over "DRUNKEN COLORED EXCURSIONISTS FIRE ON WHITE PEOPLE," which stressed that the whites were unarmed and called the passengers "shabby and ill-mannered." The Big Stone Post, in southwest Virginia, reprinted that story on August 22 under a headline about "Inoffending White People in Accomac County."

The Evening Star headed its account "WHITES AND NEGROES FIGHT," pairing a story that listed Black injuries with an Onancock dispatch blaming "the bad conduct of the negroes." The Wilmington Evening Journal repeated that dispatch after describing the excursionists as "Baltimore negro roughs." By contrast, the Alexandria Gazette's one-sentence item on a "general fight" listed only Black injuries, and Der Deutsche Correspondent had the white men begin the brick-throwing. Apart from the Gazette's brief, every account described the excursionists as drunken or disorderly, and none quoted a Black participant.

The Onancock dispatch in the Evening Star and the Evening Journal said one passenger "grossly insulted a young white girl" and was knocked down by a young white man, after which the whole crowd joined in. The Dispatch's correspondent mentioned no girl; he wrote that a drunken passenger tried to pull a white boy off a wharf pile and that a young white man then struck at a cursing passenger with a cane. Der Deutsche Correspondent said a passenger made an offensive remark about several white women, after which the men present pelted the passengers with bricks and those aboard fired revolvers.

reader.title: Onancock wharf riot
bases: A crowd of white townsmen (fifteen to fifty) fought a party of about four hundred Black excursionists at a steamboat wharf with stones and bricks, injuring several, while the passengers threw missiles and fired pistols (A1, A2, A3, A5).

Four separately sourced reports (a Baltimore-sourced story and an Onancock dispatch in A1, the Alexandria brief A2, the Richmond special A3, and the Baltimore German report A5) agree on a fight between whites and Black excursionists at the Onancock wharf on Sunday, August 17, though they disagree on its cause and casualties.

accounts.label: Baltimore-sourced wire story
accounts.gist: A party of white men on the wharf got into a disturbance with half a dozen Black passengers; stones and pistol shots followed, one Black man was shot through the shoulder, two had heads split, several whites were slightly hurt, and no arrests were made.

accounts.label: Onancock special dispatch (Evening Star / Evening Journal)
accounts.gist: Drunken passengers jostled and swore at whites and one grossly insulted a young white girl; a young white man knocked him down and the whole crowd joined in.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch Onancock correspondent
accounts.gist: A drunken passenger tried to pull a white boy off a wharf pile; after passengers cursed the whites, a young white man struck at one with a cane, and the passengers threw missiles and fired pistols at unarmed whites, who replied with brickbats.

accounts.label: Der Deutsche Correspondent (Baltimore)
accounts.gist: A crowd gathered to watch noisy passengers; after one made an offensive remark about white women, the men pelted the passengers with bricks, and those aboard fired revolvers; no one was known to be wounded.

accounts.label: Alexandria Gazette brief
accounts.gist: A general fight between the excursionists and about fifty white men in which two Black people were struck by missiles and a Black man was shot through the hand.

framing.detail: Headed 'A NEGRO OUTRAGE' with 'DRUNKEN COLORED EXCURSIONISTS FIRE ON WHITE PEOPLE' and 'Sunday Desecration'; stresses that the whites were unarmed and calls the passengers 'shabby and ill-mannered'.
Reprinted the Richmond special under a headline about 'Inoffending White People in Accomac County'.
'WHITES AND NEGROES FIGHT' lists Black injuries but calls the passengers 'some of the toughest characters in Baltimore' and closes with the Onancock dispatch blaming 'the bad conduct of the negroes'.
Calls the excursionists 'Baltimore negro roughs' who 'began insulting the white people' and repeats the girl-insult dispatch.
A one-sentence 'general fight' item listing only Black injuries.
Describes the passengers as noisy and the provocation as an offensive remark, but has the white men begin the brick-throwing.
